title: Comparison of traditional and ecological dynamical training approaches in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu: effects on Force Development, reactivity, and distress perception
authors: Giuseppe Giardullo, Rosario Ceruso, Giuseppe Di Lascio, Manuele Taleb, Giovanni Esposito, and Francesca D’Elia

population.ageGroup: amateur and semi-professional BJJ athletes ages 18–40

intervention.description: Ecological-dynamical training compared with a traditional approach

tested: Force development, response time to a light stimulus, and self-reported distress after the training period.
found: The ecological-dynamical group improved more on the measured force, light-response, and distress outcomes in this sample.
notTested: Live grappling skill, delayed retention, transfer to new situations, children, beginners, or Sensei Sandy BJJ classes. The distress questionnaire was ad hoc and had no external psychometric validation.
supports: A bounded report of the measured outcomes in these adult athletes
doesNotSupport: Claims of better live grappling skill or long-term learning
cardSummary: After eight weeks, the game group had a bigger drop in distress scores and gains on some tests.
cardLimit: The study did not test live BJJ skill or how long skills last. It did not study kids, new learners, or our school.
keywords: bjj, ecological dynamics, training approaches, force development, sensei sandy

title: The effect of game-based approaches on decision-making, knowledge, and motor skill: A systematic review and a multilevel meta-analysis
authors: Manninen M, Magrum E, Campbell S, and Belton S
sport: Physical education and sport; sports varied across studies

population.ageGroup: physical education learners across included studies

intervention.description: Games-based teaching approaches in physical education and sport

tested: Outcomes included game decision-making, motor-skill tests, knowledge, and motor skill during games.
found: The review reported better game-decision and motor-skill test results, but not better knowledge or motor skill measured during games.
notTested: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu classes or Sensei Sandy BJJ teaching. Findings do not establish one best approach for every learner or sport.
supports: A qualified summary of selected physical-education outcomes across the included studies
doesNotSupport: One teaching approach winning in every setting
cardLabel: Review of studies · other sports · 28 studies · 2024/2025
cardSummary: A review of 28 studies with 1,600 people found gains on some game-choice and skill tests.
cardLimit: Not every test showed a gain. These studies were not about BJJ.
displaySubtitle: How games help kids and adults learn movement skills.
keywords: games-based teaching review, games based teaching, games-based learning, motor skills review
humanGuide:
Simple Guide for Families & Beginners

How Games Help Us Learn

Games help people learn fast. Kids and adults both learn best through fun play. A game gives you a clear goal. You try a move right away. Your partner gives you a real puzzle. You test what works and adapt. This builds balance, poise, and quiet calm. Each class uses games that match your skill. You train with kind partners who look out for you. Coaches guide each step. You learn at your own pace from day one. Every student leaves feeling strong and capable. You feel welcome here. We help you learn. Mats are clean. Smiles are warm. You can do it.

What We Practice in Class

We play smart games on the mat. One partner tries to pass the guard. The other partner works to keep balance. Everyone stays safe. You learn to stay calm when someone moves. You learn to use mechanical leverage. You build quiet self-assurance. Parents love watching their kids have fun. Adults enjoy the friendly, cooperative room. You practice real martial arts with smiles and high fives. It feels great.

How This Connects to Our Academy

This paper reviewed twenty-eight studies in school sports. The research showed that games help people make good choices. Games also help people test their physical skills. At our studio, we use coached games every single day. We make sure practice is safe, cooperative, and fun. Beginners are always welcome to start here. You can meet Sandy for a Free First Visit. You can watch a class and see how our games work. We are glad to help.

Our Mat Culture

We are here for you. Our room is calm. Our mats are soft and clean. You will have fun. We take our time. Kids make new friends. Coaches help each child. We step on the mat together. We bow and smile. You learn real moves. You gain good balance. Partners help each other. We cheer for your wins. We love to see you grow. We love what we do.

Who Can Join

Kids can join us. Teens can join us. Adults can join us. New students start each week. Beginners are welcome from day one. You start right where you are. We meet you at your level. You move with care. You learn at your pace. We are glad you are here.

Common Questions About Games in Class

Why do kids like games on the mat? Games feel like fun play. Kids stay focused and happy. They learn to listen and move well. They make great friends in class.

Can adults learn through games too? Yes. Adults learn very well with games. Games give you a clear goal. You practice real moves with calm, relaxed grips. You build skill step by step.

Is it safe to play these games? Yes. Safety always comes first. Coaches watch every group. Partners move with care and control. You can always pause or ask questions. We help you stay safe.

How do I start? You can text Sandy or book online. Come visit our studio in Tannersville. Try a Free First Visit and see our classes in action. We look forward to meeting you.

title: How do students learn to move? A systematic review of collaborative and game-based pedagogies in physical education
authors: Saha S, İlbak İ, Abdi E, Deutsch J, Katanić B, Choudhary S, Choudhary PK, Souza LN, Silva Júnior RR, and Tornóczky GJ
sport: Physical education; sports varied across studies

population.ageGroup: physical education and PETE participants in included studies

intervention.description: Game-based and comparison teaching approaches in physical education

tested: Motor-skill and game-performance results across quasi-experimental PE/PETE studies.
found: Seven studies reported significant motor or game-performance improvement, five reported mixed results, and five found no motor-skill advantage. Methods and outcomes varied; there was no pooled effect estimate.
notTested: BJJ classes or Sensei Sandy BJJ teaching. The varied evidence does not identify one approach that wins in all settings.
supports: A cautious summary of varied PE/PETE study results
cardLabel: Review of studies · other sports · 17 studies · 2026
cardSummary: Seven studies found gains, five had mixed results, and five found no motor-skill edge.
cardLimit: The studies used many games and tests. They did not study BJJ.
keywords: pe-games-review-2026, pe, games, review, physical education, collaborative pedagogies

title: Effects of a school-based Brazilian jiu-jitsu programme on mental health and classroom behaviour of children from Abu Dhabi: a randomised trial

intervention.description: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu compared with regular physical education

tested: Teacher-rated behavioral outcomes in one Abu Dhabi school program.
found: Teacher-rated emotional symptoms (p=.007), hyperactivity and inattention (p<.001), total difficulties (p=.002), and externalizing behavior (p=.001, η²=.07) differed on selected measures.
notTested: ADHD treatment, every child, or Sensei Sandy BJJ classes. Results do not promise an individual outcome.
supports: Selected teacher-rated behavioral outcomes in this study population
authors: Jean Carlo Benetti Bueno, Leonardo Vidal Andreato, Rodrigo Batalha Silva, and Alexandro Andrade
cardLabel: BJJ study · 2022 online / 2023 issue · 88 enrolled · 80 analyzed
cardSummary: In one school study, some teacher-rated behavior scores differed between BJJ and PE groups.
cardLimit: This was one school study of boys. It used teacher reports. It did not test our school or show what each child will gain.
detailedResults: The reported values were p=.007 for emotional symptoms, p<.001 for hyperactivity/inattention, p=.002 for total difficulties, and p=.001 with η²=.07 for externalizing behavior.
keywords: school-based bjj, mental health, classroom behaviour, randomised trial, youth bjj

title: Injury prevalence among Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu practitioners globally: a cross-sectional study in 881 participants
authors: Pablo Martin Stegerhoek, Boris Brajovic, Paul Kuijer, and Mirwais Mehrab

population.ageGroup: BJJ practitioners; mean age 30.8 years (SD 8.6); 817 participants were male

intervention.description: Retrospective survey of global BJJ practitioners who trained at least weekly, covering training, competition, and injuries in the prior 12 months

tested: Self-reported injuries. An injury meant medical care, at least one week away from training, or at least two weeks of modified training.
found: The 881 participants reported 888 injuries. Rates were 5.5 per 1,000 training hours and 55.9 per 1,000 matches. Of the injuries, 789 (89%) happened in training; 620 of those (79%) happened during sparring. Knees accounted for 223 injuries (25%) and shoulders for 114 (13%).
notTested: Prospective injury causes, whether prevention practices work, individual risk, youth injury rates, or injury rates at Sensei Sandy BJJ.
supports: Describing self-reported injury patterns and rates in this surveyed population
doesNotSupport: A Sensei Sandy BJJ injury rate
keywords: bjj injury prevalence, global study, safety in bjj, practitioners survey
